newsitem.title: CANADA: World wheat prices slide on European rains - CWB.
newsitem.headline: World wheat prices slide on European rains - CWB.

text.p: World wheat prices should continue their slide due to rains on drought-stressed European crops, a Canadian Wheat Board market analyst said on Monday.

"The wheat's down C$5 to C$6 a tonne. The key factor is the drought's over in Europe, they've had two to three inches of rain over the past couple of weeks, so the yield prospects look good for wheat," CWB market analyst Larry Sawatzky said.
The CWB cut back its world price estimate by C$5 a tonne Thursday for benchmark No1 Canada Western Red Spring wheat to C$171.00-C$201.00 a tonne in-store Vancouver or St. Lawrence.
That is down 2.6 percent from April's world price estimate for No1 CWRS at C$176.00-C$206.00 while U.S. hard red winter wheat futures have fallen 10 percent since late April.
"They (Europe) are expected to have the same size wheat crop they had this year and they had a record wheat crop this year," Sawatzky said.
Europe harvested a 98-million-tonne wheat crop in the 1996/97 (July/June) crop year, Sawatzky said.
Another bearish supply factor was U.S. winter wheat output. A late April frost threatened U.S. production prospects.

"The U.S. winter wheat harvest is underway and the harvest pressure is starting to kick in and the frost damage in hard red winter wheat area is starting to look like it wasn't as severe as the market was expecting," Sawatzky said.

May wheat futures set a 10-month high of US$5.14 a bushel on April 21 at the Kansas City Board of Trade on reports of crop losses from a freeze on the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter wheat region and Europe's drought.
The previous high was set at US$5.17 on June 18, 1996 and the contract high was set at US$5.75 on May 8, 1996 when world stocks were near a 20-year low.
KCBT's hard red winter May wheat contract expired May 20 at US$4.61-1/2 a bushel, down 10 percent from April 21.
While supply appeared to be assured, demand should remain level through the summer.
"Demand had been quite sluggish until recently. A lot of buyers were buying hand-to-mouth but with the drop in price we have seen buyers come back to the market to cover themselves," Sawatzky said.
"China is not expected to be a factor over the summer. We're expecting them to have an even larger crop than the record this (crop) year," Sawatzky said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture on May 12 set Chinese wheat output at 114 million tonnes for crop year 1997/98.

"We're expecting a little lower than that, maybe two to three million tonnes lower than that but that would still be higher than this year's record, their crop this (crop) year was around 109 million tonnes," Sawatzky said.
The only exception to slack demand through the summer may prove to be Iran.
"A positive factor is Iran. We're expecting Iran to be another big market in the upcoming year," Sawatzky said.
Iran bought an average 3.485 million tonnes since 1986.
The International Grains Council forecast on May 1 that Iran's import needs in the 12 months ending June 30, 1997 should total 6.6 million tonnes.
That would make Iran the world's biggest wheat importer ahead of Egypt and Japan at 6.2 and 6.0 million tonnes respectively. China has usually been the biggest importer.
"Their imports doubled this year. I'm not going to say exactly how much we expect them to import in the upcoming year but we expect them to continue to be a big buyer, a major factor," Sawatzky said.
"It'll probably be a little lower than that (6.6 million tonnes) in 1997/98," Sawatzky added.
((Winnipeg Reuters bureau 204 947 3548))
